title: tsdb: harden head-chunk cache lifecycle
body:
Collapse the cache fingerprint into a comparable `headChunkCacheKey` so the hit check, populate, and reset are single expressions and future fingerprint fields cannot be forgotten in the comparison.

Bound the cache buffer: apply the `headChunksBufMaxCap` policy when moving to a different series, pre-size replacement collections from `headChunkCount`, and release the cache on `Close`. Route the OOO wrapper's cache enablement and `Close` through the `headChunkReader` methods and release its fallback collection buffer on `Close`, and propagate chunk reader `Close` errors in the head-and-OOO queriers.

Zero the collection tail inside `collectHeadChunks` itself instead of at every call site, and document the contract there.

Test the cache-hit path with a sentinel (a re-collection for the same series rewrites the same backing array, so pointer identity of the slice cannot distinguish a hit from a miss), extract a shared test-head helper, and assert outside the series lock so a failing assertion cannot deadlock the cleanup's `Close`.

title: tsdb: fix stale head-chunk cache after head-chunk truncation (#19134)
body:
Backport of #19134 to `release-3.13`.

The head-chunk cache fingerprint (series ref, head pointer, mmapped count) could not detect `truncateChunksBefore` removing older head chunks: the head pointer survives and, for a series with no mmapped chunks, the mmapped count stays 0, while `firstChunkID` advances. A cache-enabled reader (range queries through the head-and-OOO reader) then resolved chunk IDs against the stale slice and returned the wrong chunk, or failed with `ErrNotFound`.

Include `firstChunkID` in the fingerprint; it advances on every truncation and never regresses.

The head-chunk cache (#18302) that introduced the bug is present in `release-3.13`, so the fix applies. Cherry-picked cleanly from commit 39359eb784397136c1aa91046915ca6c2ec93b42; the `headChunkReader` struct and `getOrCollectHeadChunks` are byte-identical between `main` and `release-3.13`.

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] TSDB: Fix the head-chunk cache returning samples from the wrong chunk, or spurious not-found errors, to range queries after head-chunk truncation
```

Backport of commit 827d0f9ad ("ci: run version upgrade test as a per-LTS matrix") to `release-3.13`.

On `release-3.13`, `TestVersionUpgrade_UpgradeDowngradeLatestLTS` runs every active LTS release sequentially within a single CI job. title: chore(tsdb): simplify cutSegmentFile by removing temp file indirection
body:
This will allow the simplification of the directIOWriter.

PR #7573 introduced a .tmp file + rename pattern in cutSegmentFile to prevent mmap from seeing empty files after a crash. However, without an fsync on the file itself, a crash could still leave the renamed file with zero content or sth else. PR #8061 added repairLastChunkFile as the real fix, extended in PR #11338 to detect zero magic numbers.

The .tmp indirection is redundant, both callers have crash safety:

- Head chunks: repairLastChunkFile removes corrupt last files on startup. No intermediary broken file can exist (handleChunkWriteError panics, so the corrupt file is always the last one).
- Compaction: files live in a .tmp-for-creation block directory, cleaned up entirely on failure or restart.

Remove the pattern for fewer syscalls and a simpler write path.

title: rules: delete remaining rule_group metrics on group removal
body:
#### Description

When a rule group is removed or renamed on config reload, `Manager.Update` deletes the `rule_group`-labeled series for the group metrics, but two metrics carrying the same `rule_group` label were missed:

- `GroupLastRuleDurationSum` (`rule_group_last_rule_duration_sum_seconds`)
- `GroupLastRestoreDuration` (`rule_group_last_restore_duration_seconds`)

Both are `GaugeVec`s labeled by `rule_group` and set per group (on every evaluation and on restore respectively), so their series were never cleaned up. Every reload that dropped or renamed a group leaked two stale series per group, growing memory and `/metrics` cardinality over time.

This adds the two missing `DeleteLabelValues` calls next to the existing cleanup, and extends `TestMetricsUpdate` to include `rule_group_last_rule_duration_sum_seconds`. The test fails without the fix (the dropped group's series remain) and passes with it.

#### Testing

`go test ./rules/ -run TestMetricsUpdate` passes with the fix and fails without it.

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] Rules: Delete the `rule_group_last_rule_duration_sum_seconds` and `rule_group_last_restore_duration_seconds` series when a rule group is removed or renamed on reload.
```

title: fix: accept empty HELP text without trailing space in OpenMetrics parser
body:
The OpenMetrics lexer rejects valid `# HELP metric_name` lines when there's no trailing space after the metric name. The `sMeta2` state only has a rule requiring at least one space character before the newline, so a bare newline causes a parse error.

The OpenMetrics spec says HELP text "SHOULD be non-empty" (not MUST), so empty HELP metadata is valid.

Adds a new lexer rule to handle the bare newline case in `sMeta2`, plus a test case.

Related: #12202

body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:
Fixes #18273

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-notes
[ENHANCEMENT] cmd/prometheus: Extract main() logic into reusable run(ctx, args, reg) function to enable in-process testing and benchmarking.
```

## Summary

This PR extracts the Prometheus server startup logic from `main()` into a new `run(ctx context.Context, args []string, reg prometheus.Registerer) error` function, enabling in-process testing and benchmarking without spawning a separate process.

### Key changes

- **New `run()` function**: contains all startup logic and accepts:
  - `ctx context.Context` — cancellation support (`<-ctx.Done()` in termination handler allows programmatic shutdown)
  - `args []string` — CLI args (like `os.Args[1:]`), avoiding coupling to `os.Args`
  - `reg prometheus.Registerer` — metrics registry, enabling isolated registries in tests
- **New `ExitError` type**: carries an exit code through the error return, so `main()` preserves `os.Exit()` codes
- **Removed package-level globals**: `agentMode`, `agentOnlyFlags`, `serverOnlyFlags`, `configSuccess`, `configSuccessTime` are now local to `run()`
- **Updated `reloadConfig()`**: takes `agentMode`, `configSuccess`, `configSuccessTime` as parameters instead of globals
- **Simplified `main()`**: sets up the GoCollector, creates a context, and delegates to `run()`

### Backwards compatibility

All existing subprocess-based tests (`-test.main` pattern) continue to work unchanged.

### Example usage in tests/benchmarks

```go
func BenchmarkMain(b *testing.B) {
    for b.Loop() {
        reg := prometheus.NewRegistry()
        ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
        go func() { time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond); cancel() }()
        _ = run(ctx, []string{
            "--config.file=testdata/prometheus.yml",
            "--web.listen-address=0.0.0.0:0",
            "--storage.tsdb.path=" + b.TempDir(),
        }, reg)
    }
}
```

title: tsdb: fix goroutine leaks when Open() fails on corrupt data
body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Reported by https://github.com/grafana/mimir/pull/14672.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] TSDB: Fix goroutine and file handle leaks when `tsdb.Open()` fails on corrupt `chunks_head` data.
```

When `tsdb.Open()` fails due to corrupt `chunks_head` files, several resources started before the failure were never cleaned up:

- `NewChunkDiskMapper` starts a `writeQueue` goroutine and opens the `chunks_head` directory handle. If `openMMapFiles()` fails, the mapper is discarded by `NewHead`; the goroutine keeps running and the directory handle stays open (on Windows this prevents directory removal).
- WAL/WBL goroutines are started before `NewHead`. When `NewHead` fails, `db.head` is nil, so `db.Close()` skips `head.Close()` and the WAL goroutines are never stopped.
- The lockfile is acquired before `NewHead`. On the error path, `db.donec` is closed before `db.Close()` runs, so `db.Close()` short-circuits and `db.locker.Release()` is never called, leaking the flock handle and leaving the `lock` file behind.

Fix by:
- Stopping the `writeQueue` and closing the directory handle in `NewChunkDiskMapper` when `openMMapFiles` fails.
- Closing WAL/WBL explicitly in the error defer when `db.head` was never initialized.
- Releasing the locker explicitly in the error defer.

title: tsdb: handle Close() errors in querier cleanup defers
body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Fixes #19114

---

### What this PR does

This PR handles the previously ignored `Close()` errors in the cleanup paths of `Querier()` and `blockChunkQuerierForRange()` in `tsdb/db.go`.

Previously, both cleanup blocks discarded errors returned from closing block queriers:

```go
for _, q := range blockQueriers {
    _ = q.Close()
}
```

These cleanup paths run while the function is already returning an error. If closing a querier also failed, that additional failure was lost.

This change uses `errors.Join()` to preserve the original error while also returning any cleanup errors:

```go
if closeErr := q.Close(); closeErr != nil {
    err = errors.Join(err, fmt.Errorf("close querier during cleanup: %w", closeErr))
}
```

This keeps the existing error behavior while providing more context when cleanup fails. The successful path remains unchanged.

---

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] TSDB: Preserve querier Close() errors during cleanup instead of silently discarding them.

title: fix(discovery/oci): clear targets of vanished compartments
body:
The SD emitted one target group per compartment, keyed by compartment OCID. The discovery manager only drops a target group's source when an empty group is sent for it, so with compartment auto-discovery a compartment that was deleted or is no longer returned by compartment listing left its last targets behind until Prometheus restarted.

Merge all compartments into a single target group instead. Emitting one static source per refresh lets the manager replace the whole target set every cycle, so vanished instances simply disappear with no per-compartment bookkeeping. The owning compartment stays available on each target via the __meta_oci_compartment_id label.

#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

None.

#### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered).

The doc comments on `bucketLimitAppender` and `bucketLimitAppenderV2` were copied
from `limitAppender` and never updated. They claim to "limit the number of total
appended samples in a batch", but neither type counts samples: both cap the number
of buckets in native histograms, reducing the histogram resolution (via
`ReduceResolution`) or returning `errBucketLimit` when the limit is exceeded.

`bucketLimitAppender.AppendHistogram` and `bucketLimitAppenderV2.Append` have no
per-batch sample counter (only a `limit int`); they compare
`len(h.PositiveBuckets)+len(h.NegativeBuckets)` against `limit`. This is the same
copied text that was already correct on `limitAppender` (which does count samples
and returns `errSampleLimit`), so the comment reads plausibly but describes the
wrong appender.

Two of the comments also named the wrong type after the AppenderV2 additions:

- `limitAppenderV2` started `// limitAppender ...` (its behaviour text was already
  correct; only the leading identifier was wrong).
- `bucketLimitAppenderV2` started `// bucketLimitAppender ...` (wrong on both the
  identifier and the behaviour text).

This corrects all three so each doc comment starts with the type it documents and
accurately describes bucket limiting. No behaviour change.

title: tsdb: fix flaky TestQuerierShouldNotFailIfOOOCompactionOccurs* tests
body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Part of #17941 (the remaining `TestQuerierShouldNotFailIfOOOCompactionOccursAfterRetrievingQuerier_AppendV2` / `_Iterators_AppendV2` Windows item; intentionally not `Fixes` so the meta issue stays open).

#### What this PR does:

All six `TestQuerierShouldNotFailIfOOOCompactionOccurs*` tests (three in `db_test.go`, three `_AppendV2` variants) wait at most **one second** for `CompactOOOHead` to complete after closing the blocking querier:

```go
require.Eventually(t, compactionComplete.Load, time.Second, 10*time.Millisecond, ...)
```

That window sits right at the failure boundary by construction: the compaction goroutine only notices the querier close by **polling in 500ms intervals** (`WaitForPendingReadersForOOOChunksAtOrBefore`, [head.go#L1393-L1397](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/tsdb/head.go#L1393-L1397)), and after it notices it still has to garbage collect chunks and truncate the WBL. On slow Windows CI runners that regularly exceeds one second, producing the failures posted in #17941.

Two changes, test-only:

1. **Widen the `require.Eventually` window from 1s to 1min.** `Eventually` returns as soon as the condition holds, so fast runners lose nothing; slow runners stop flaking.
2. **Move the `require` calls out of the compaction goroutine.** `require` must not be called from non-test goroutines (`t.FailNow` only works on the test goroutine). This is also what produced the confusing secondary `compact ooo head: populate block: context canceled` failures in the CI logs: after the `Eventually` timeout failed the test, cleanup closed the DB, and the still-running goroutine's `require.NoError` fired with the cancellation error. The goroutine now reports its error through a channel and all assertions (including the `chunksRemoved` metric check) happen on the test goroutine after completion.

The initial `time.Sleep(time.Second)` + `require.False` (asserting compaction blocks while the querier is open) is left untouched — its semantics are unaffected.

#### Verification

Ran natively on **Windows** (the platform where the flake reproduces): all six tests, three runs each, green (`go test ./tsdb/ -run "TestQuerierShouldNotFailIfOOOCompactionOccurs" -count=3`).

title: discovery/moby: guard nil ContainerSpec for non-container swarm services
body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

No existing issue; this is a self-contained crash fix found while reading the
Docker Swarm service discovery code.

Docker Swarm service discovery builds the per-service label map in
`refreshServices` by dereferencing `s.Spec.TaskTemplate.ContainerSpec`
unconditionally for the container hostname and image labels:

```go
swarmLabelServiceTaskContainerHostname: s.Spec.TaskTemplate.ContainerSpec.Hostname,
swarmLabelServiceTaskContainerImage:    s.Spec.TaskTemplate.ContainerSpec.Image,
```

In the moby SDK, `swarm.TaskSpec.ContainerSpec` is an optional pointer
(`*ContainerSpec`, `json:",omitempty"`) that is mutually exclusive with
`PluginSpec` and `NetworkAttachmentSpec`: it is `nil` when a service's task
runtime is `plugin` (a Docker managed plugin deployed via Swarm) or `attachment`
(a Swarm network-attachment task). `ServiceList` returns those services with no
runtime filtering, so a `nil` `ContainerSpec` reaches the label map and panics
with a nil pointer dereference, which aborts the entire services refresh (there
is no per-service recover).

This mirrors the guard the sibling task path already applies at
`discovery/moby/tasks.go` (`if s.Spec.ContainerSpec != nil`), and the same
function already guards the other optional pointer, `s.UpdateStatus`.

The fix sets the container hostname and image labels only when `ContainerSpec`
is non-nil. Plugin and network-attachment services simply omit those two labels
(other service labels are unaffected). A regression test adds a plugin service
with `ContainerSpec == nil` alongside a normal container service; before the fix
it panics, after the fix it returns both targets with the container labels
present for the normal service and absent for the plugin service.

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] Discovery: Do not panic in Docker Swarm service discovery when a service has no container spec (plugin or network-attachment runtime).
```

title: [Proposal] promql: add evaluation‑time aligned subqueries [range::step]
body:
Fixes #9767 PromQL can already express aligned historical lookbacks, but today they usually mean a hand-written chain of `offset`s. This PR follows the direction discussed in #9767 and #9114. It adds an experimental subquery form, `[range::step]`, which evaluates a subquery on a grid aligned to the evaluation time. Enable it with `--enable-feature=promql-eval-aligned-subqueries`. Today, if you want a daily baseline for a signal such as request rate, you usually have to write it by hand with `offset`s: ```promql ( rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 0d) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 1d) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 2d) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 3d) ) / 4 ``` This works today, but it gets heavy very quickly once you want aligned historical lookbacks to be a normal building block in larger queries. With this PR, that becomes: ```promql avg_over_time(rate(http_requests_total[5m])[3d::1d]) ``` ### Real use cases This is useful when you want to: - build a daily or weekly baseline for traffic, latency, or error rate - compare the current signal with the same time slot on previous days, instead of with a global average - write alerts that are aware of daily or weekly traffic patterns - check whether a spike after a deploy is a real regression or just the usual traffic shape for that time of day So the user value is simple: - aligned historical lookbacks become a first-class PromQL pattern - queries that are now written as long lists of `offset`s become shorter and easier to compose ### The idea PromQL already has `[range:step]`. This PR adds `[range::step]`. The difference is the sampling grid. - `[range:step]` uses the usual epoch-aligned grid: `..., 0, step, 2*step, ...` - `[range::step]` uses a grid aligned to the effective evaluation time: `..., E-2*step, E-step, E` The window itself doesn't change. It's still `(E-range, E]`. ### A small example Take this case: - `E = 50s` - `range = 30s` - `step = 20s` - window `(20s, 50s]` ```text time: 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 window: (--------------] : ticks: 0--------20--------40--------60 -> picks {40} :: ticks: 10--------30--------50 -> picks {30,50} ``` So `:` and `::` use the same window, but they pick different timestamps from it. ### How it works - `t` is the evaluation timestamp: - for an instant query, the query time - for a range query, the current outer step timestamp - `offset` shifts the effective evaluation time backwards - `@ ` pins the effective evaluation time to a fixed timestamp - `@ start()` and `@ end()` keep their existing meaning So the effective evaluation time `E` is: - without `@`: `E = t - offset` - with `@ `: `E = - offset` Two useful consequences: - with `::` and `step > 0`, `E` is always on the sampling grid - `[range::]` uses the same default step as `[range:]` ### Range queries This is the tricky part. `query_range` doesn't evaluate at every timestamp between `start` and `end`. It evaluates on the outer step grid: ```text start, start+step, start+2*step, ... ``` and returns the timestamps on that grid that are `<= end`. Example: - `start = 0s` - `end = 25s` - `step = 10s` ```text request: [0s -------------------------------- 25s] step grid: 0s 10s 20s 30s eval t: 0s 10s 20s returned: ^ ^ ^ raw end: 25s (not evaluated) ``` So this range query returns results for `0s`, `10s`, and `20s`. `25s` is inside the requested time range, but it is not on the outer step grid, so the expression is not evaluated there. For `::`, that means the anchor has to be the last actual evaluated timestamp, not raw `end`. In this example: - anchoring to raw `end = 25s` would shift the aligned inner grid to `..., 5s, 15s, 25s` - but the last returned outer step is `20s`, so the last aligned evaluation has to be anchored to `20s` That keeps `query_range` consistent with running the equivalent instant query at each returned step. ### The implementation idea For `:`, the inner sampling grid is fixed, so for a range query the engine can keep reusing the same phase across outer steps. For `::`, that is not true. The aligned grid is tied to the effective evaluation time, so in a range query it usually moves at every outer step. Take an outer range query with step `10s`, and an inner aligned subquery with step `3s`: ```text outer eval t: 100s 110s 120s anchor 100s -> 91 94 97 100 anchor 110s -> 101 104 107 110 anchor 120s -> 111 114 117 120 ``` The window shape stays the same, but the phase changes with the outer evaluation timestamp. That means the engine can't pick one aligned phase for the whole range query and reuse it everywhere. That was the main trap in the earlier attempt. So the implementation idea is: - for each outer step, use that step's own effective evaluation time as the anchor - keep the full inner window when needed, instead of reducing it as if the phase were fixed - filter the available inner points to the timestamps that belong to that outer step's aligned grid - if nested aligned subqueries use steps that don't line up cleanly, evaluate densely enough internally so the needed aligned points exist for every outer step In other words, the engine doesn't treat `::` as a single global alignment choice for the whole range query. It treats alignment as part of each outer evaluation step. If `@` pins the effective evaluation time to a fixed timestamp, then the anchor stops moving, and this becomes simpler again. ### Cost This isn't free, but it is opt-in. Existing queries keep their current behavior and cost model. This only affects queries that explicitly use `::`. - With `:`, the sampling grid is fixed, so the engine can reduce the buffered window between outer steps. - With `::`, the grid moves with `E`, so the engine has to keep the full window and filter it per outer step. - If aligned subqueries are nested and inner and outer steps don't line up, the engine may need a finer internal step so the right aligned points exist for every outer step. So the trade-off is local and explicit: `::` is more expressive, and in some cases more expensive. ### Testing PromQL tests cover: - direct `:` vs `::` differences - `@`, including `@ start()` and `@ end()` - fixed `@ ` in range queries, including non-divisible inner and outer steps - range queries where raw `end` isn't on a step boundary - `[range::]` with the default step - nested aligned subqueries - histogram behavior in both instant and range mode - non-divisible inner and outer steps
One aligned query and its hand-written equivalent ```promql ( rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 0m) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 10m) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 20m) ) / 3 avg_over_time(rate(http_requests_total[5m])[30m::10m]) ``` ```promql ( rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 0m) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 10m) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 20m) + rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 30m) ) / 4 avg_over_time(avg_over_time(rate(http_requests_total[5m])[20m::10m])[40m::20m]) ```
```release-notes [FEATURE] PromQL: Add evaluation-time aligned subqueries [range::step]. ```

title: promql: detect and warn on overlapping start timestamps
body:
### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Fixes #18534

### Description

This PR implements query-time detection of overlapping start timestamp windows for both delta and cumulative counter metrics.

**Problem:**
Metrics with start timestamps can have overlapping time spans when a sample's start timestamp (ST) is earlier than the previous sample's timestamp (T). This indicates potential data quality issues such as:

- Clock skew or time synchronization problems
- Out-of-order sample ingestion
- Misconfigured exporters
- Application restarts with incorrect state

Some monitoring systems reject these samples outright, but Prometheus currently accepts them silently, which can lead to incorrect query results.

**Solution:**
This PR adds query-time warnings using Prometheus's annotation mechanism to alert users when overlapping start timestamp spans are detected during rate(), increase(), and related calculations.

**Implementation:**

- Adds StartTimeOverlapWarning annotation type with intelligent merging (counts occurrences per metric)
- Implements checkStartTimeOverlap() helper function with overlap detection logic that works for both delta temporality (OTel-style) and cumulative counters
- Detects overlaps in extrapolatedRate() and histogramRate() functions for float and histogram samples
- Emits warning once per series to avoid spam
- Handles nil/zero start timestamps gracefully (no false positives)
- Optimized: only extracts metric names when warnings are needed

**Overlap Detection Condition:**
An overlap is detected when: currST != 0 AND currST < prevT AND currST != prevST

This condition correctly identifies overlaps for:
- **Delta counters**: where ST should equal previous T (e.g., OTel delta temporality)
- **Cumulative counters**: where ST should remain constant across samples

**Testing:**

- Unit tests for annotation creation, merging, and deduplication (util/annotations)
- Comprehensive integration tests using promqltest with multiple scenarios:
  - Valid delta timeseries (no warning)
  - Valid cumulative counters (no warning)
  - Samples without start timestamps (no warning)
  - Invalid overlapping start timestamps (warning expected)
  - Mixed queries with label selectors

**Dependencies:**
This PR builds on the start timestamp infrastructure from #18344 (merged), which propagates StartTimestamps through the query evaluation path.

### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered).

```release-notes
[FEATURE] PromQL: Add query-time warning when samples have overlapping start timestamps (applicable to both delta and cumulative counters).
